problem: Deep RL for outdoor point-goal navigation in unstructured terrain is sample-inefficient and hard to generalize, and there is little systematic comparison of standard RL algorithms on such tasks in photorealistic simulation.
motivation: Real-world RL training is costly and risky, so photorealistic simulation is needed. The authors want a privileged-information expert policy that can later be distilled into a vision-based policy, and first need to know which standard RL algorithm trains it best.
key_idea: Benchmark PPO, A2C, SAC and TD3 (stable-baselines3) on a privileged-state point-goal navigation task with obstacles in the MIDGARD Unreal Engine 5 simulator.
insight: On-policy PPO was the most stable and successful (~65% success). A2C plateaued at ~30%, SAC at ~20% and TD3 at ~12%. The authors attribute this to PPO's clipped updates and to off-policy replay buffers struggling with non-stationary data and exploration, but they ran no ablations or hyperparameter sweeps, so that explanation is a hypothesis. Success rates come from training curves only (Fig. 4).
method: Task/MDP: point-goal navigation in a forest scene, with the goal given relative to the agent and assumed reachable; 20% obstacle density; 10-20 m target distance; 2000 steps per episode
State (privileged): distance to the target, sin/cos of the angle to the target, and distance and angle to the 3 nearest obstacles, using exact obstacle positions as in Learning by Cheating
Action: continuous skid-steer velocities, v in [0,1] and ω in [-1,1]; the agent is teleported each step with non-holonomic kinematics to save compute
Reward: +5 for reaching the goal, -2 for collision, -2 for out-of-bounds, otherwise 0.1(d_t - d_{t-1}) - 0.01 per step
Policy network: MLP with two hidden layers of 64 units outputting v and ω
Training: 200 parallel agents in MIDGARD; the environment is fully reset every N steps to avoid overfitting to obstacle layouts; algorithms are SB3 implementations of PPO, A2C, SAC and TD3

setting.backbone: Small MLP (2x64) policy trained from scratch with PPO/A2C/SAC/TD3
setting.training_data: Online RL in MIDGARD forest scenes, 200 parallel agents, procedurally generated obstacles at 20% density; no extra data
setting.observation: Privileged low-dimensional state: distance and angle to goal plus distances and angles to the 3 nearest obstacles (no images)
setting.action_space: continuous linear and angular velocity (v in [0,1], ω in [-1,1])
setting.privileged: exact obstacle and goal positions used in the state

numbers_note: Results are given only as training-curve figures (Fig. 4 success rate, Fig. 5 reward). Approximate plateau values appear in the text: PPO ~65%, A2C ~30%, SAC ~20%, TD3 ~12%. These are not table values, so none are recorded.
results: PPO reaches the highest success rate, stabilizing around 65%, against roughly 30% for A2C, 20% for SAC and 12% for TD3. Reward curves follow the same ordering. No algorithm reaches an optimal policy.
limitations: Uses privileged obstacle positions and low-dimensional states, and there is no vision-based policy or sim-to-real test
Off-policy methods were not tuned and results are curves from a single setup, with no seeds, variance or tables
Only one environment (forest, 20% obstacle density) is tested, and success saturates at ~65%
